The '''1756 [[FLLA]] World Cup''' was the 22nd edition of the [[FLLA World Cup]], the quadrennial international [[Arraby]] tournament contested by the senior men's national teams of the member associations of the [[FLLA]]. It was held jointly by [[Erkizil]], [[Quidic]], [[Wundry]] and [[Ztesh]] from 9 June to 9 July 1756, and was the first FLLA World Cup ever staged in [[Quia]].<ref name="flla-summary">{{cite web|url=https://www.flla.org/world-cup/1756/tournament-report|title=1756 FLLA World Cup: official tournament report|publisher=[[FLLA]]|date=12 August 1756}}</ref> The four host associations had been awarded the tournament by the [[FLLA]] Council on 7 March 1751 in support of a unified bid coordinated by the [[QUFVL]]. Thirty-two nations qualified for the final tournament, drawn from the seven continental confederations of the [[FLLA]], and contested 64 matches across twelve host venues.<ref name="flla-summary" />

[[Quidic]] won the tournament, defeating [[New Misos]] 1–0 in the [[#Final|final]] to claim their first and only FLLA World Cup title. Quidic progressed through the competition without losing a match in normal time, topping Group B with a maximum nine points before defeating [[Terressin]], fellow hosts [[Ztesh]] and (after extra time) [[Dual Cenryia]] on the way to the final. [[Dual Cenryia]] finished third, the best result in their history, following a 3–2 win over [[Raledria]] in the third-place playoff at the Takhna Federal Stadium. Of the four host nations, only [[Quidic]] reached the final; [[Ztesh]] were eliminated in the quarter-finals by Quidic, [[Erkizil]] went out in the round of sixteen on penalties to [[Vesozata]], and [[Wundry]] became the only host to fall at the group stage, finishing third in Group H. The defending champions [[Praesyu]], winners of the [[1752 FLLA World Cup]], failed to qualify for the finals after being edged out of their [[AYFVL]] qualifying group by [[Lydroa]] on goal difference.

A total of 221 goals were scored in 64 matches at an average of 3.45 per match, one of the highest scoring rates recorded at a FLLA World Cup.<ref name="flla-summary" /> Quidic finished as the tournament's leading goalscoring nation with 22 goals, and Quidican forward Daron Veshani was awarded the FLLA Marskval with 8 personal strikes.<ref name="flla-awards">{{cite web|url=https://www.flla.org/world-cup/1756/awards|title=1756 FLLA World Cup individual and team awards|publisher=[[FLLA]]|date=10 July 1756}}</ref> The Best Player award (the FLLA Vairan Ball) was given to Quidican central midfielder Marlen Tavri, who captained the champions throughout the tournament. The competition was also notable for the introduction of the four-nation co-hosting format, which had no precedent in FLLA World Cup history.

==Host selection==
{{Main|1756 FLLA World Cup bids}}

The four-nation [[QUFVL]] bid was confirmed as host of the 1756 FLLA World Cup by the [[FLLA]] Council on 7 March 1751, ending a bidding process that had opened twenty-eight months earlier. The collective bid, formally submitted in November 1750 under the umbrella of the [[QUFVL]] secretariat, prevailed over rival proposals from [[Praesyu]], [[Raledria]] and a joint [[Trian]]–[[Seytinemas|Seytinemasi]] bid; an earlier bid from [[Iainoa]] had been withdrawn at the longlist stage in February 1750 after a domestic political crisis interrupted the country's federal infrastructure programme.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.flla.org/news/1751/host-selection-qufvl|title=QUFVL four-nation bid confirmed as 1756 hosts|publisher=[[FLLA]]|date=7 March 1751}}</ref>

The [[Quian Union]] had submitted joint bids in the spring of 1749 before withdrawing them in favour of a smaller submission under the [[QUFVL]] banner at the urging of the FLLA Council, which had cautioned against the prospect of a competitive bid from outside [[Ayuma]] being too spread out between Quian nations. The unified bid was the first joint submission of its kind in the competition's history and the first to propose distribution of matches across more than two national territories. The total infrastructure budget pledged by the four host governments and the participating municipalities was {{lahn}}1.42&nbsp;billion, of which {{lahn}}410&nbsp;million was directed towards transport upgrades, principally cross-border rail capacity between [[Nakos]], [[Talvani]] and [[Eserni]]. A separate operational budget of {{lahn}}260&nbsp;million was allocated to security, broadcasting infrastructure and the volunteer programme across the four host nations.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.qufvl.org/1756/bid-dossier|title=Four-nation 1756 FLLA World Cup bid dossier: budget and infrastructure summary|publisher=[[QUFVL]]|date=18 November 1750}}</ref>

==Participating teams and officials==

===Qualification===
{{Main|1756 FLLA World Cup qualification}}
[[File:1756 FLLA World Cup qualification.png|thumb|upright=1.5|{{legend|#000cff|Countries qualified for World Cup}} {{legend|#ffb400|Country did not qualify}} {{legend|black|Countries that did not enter the World Cup or were expelled from the tournament by FLLA prior to playing a match}} {{legend|#ababab|Country not a FLLA member}}]]

A total of 32 places at the tournament were allocated across the seven continental confederations of the [[FLLA]].<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.flla.org/world-cup/1756/qualification-allocation|title=Confederation berth allocation for the 1756 FLLA World Cup|publisher=[[FLLA]]|date=4 October 1753}}</ref> Each confederation administered its own qualifying competition, with the format reflecting the size of its membership and its allocation of finals berths. The four host associations [[Erkizil]], [[Quidic]], [[Wundry]] and [[Ztesh]] qualified as of right under FLLA hosting regulations and took the four berths reserved for the host confederation, the [[QUFVL]]. The defending champions [[Praesyu]], winners of the [[1752 FLLA World Cup]], were eliminated in [[AYFVL]] qualifying after finishing second in their group behind [[Lydroa]] on goal difference, becoming the first reigning champions to miss a FLLA World Cup finals since the expansion to 32 teams.

The qualifying tournaments are summarised below; full results are recorded on the individual confederation pages.

===Final draw===
{{Main|1756 FLLA World Cup seeding}}

The final draw for the group stage was held at the [[QUFVL]] Conference Hall in [[Talvani]] on 9 December 1755, six months before the opening match. The 32 qualified teams were divided into four pots of eight on the basis of their pre-tournament [[FLLA]] rankings, with the four hosts ([[Erkizil]], [[Quidic]], [[Wundry]], [[Ztesh]]) and the four highest-ranked non-host sides ([[Raledria]], [[Emara]], [[Verusa]] and [[New Misos]]) placed in the seeded pot. The three remaining pots were arranged on geographical lines so as to maximise the continental diversity of each group; under the procedure approved by the FLLA Organising Committee in September 1755, no group was permitted to contain more than two sides from any one confederation other than the host [[QUFVL]].<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.flla.org/1756/final-draw|title=Procedures for the 1756 FLLA World Cup final draw|publisher=[[FLLA]]|date=12 September 1755}}</ref>

The draw was conducted by FLLA general secretary Yorvan Lestrika and presented by Quidican broadcaster Karen Mihasi, with retired internationals from each of the seven confederations drawing the team names. The ceremony was televised by 32 broadcasters across more than 130 countries.

===Officials===
{{Main|1756 FLLA World Cup officials}}

The FLLA Referees Committee appointed 23 refereeing trios, each consisting of one referee and two assistants from the same national association, and five support pairs drawn from a combined pool of 19 nations. The selections were announced in two tranches between August 1755 and February 1756, following an assessment programme at the [[1755 FLLA Continental Champions Cup]] and at senior friendlies organised across the four host cities of [[Nakos]], [[Talvani]], [[Eserni]] and [[Tiraqsi]].<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.flla.org/1756/officials-announced|title=Match officials confirmed for the 1756 FLLA World Cup|publisher=[[FLLA]]|date=11 February 1756}}</ref>

The opening match was refereed by Marcus Aldrich of [[Areoix Lie]], an [[ACFVL]]-affiliated official. The final was officiated by Lassan Vetren of [[Walporein]] ([[NAFVL]]), who would later take charge of a semi-final at the [[1760 FLLA World Cup|1760 edition]]. The two semi-finals were taken by Aakash Sharma of [[Dahe]] ([[MSFVL]]) for the first semi-final and Renat Petr of [[Pelugrotoa]] ([[MAFVL]]) for the second. The 23 selected referees were drawn from 19 nations and represented all seven [[FLLA]] confederations.

==Squads==
{{Main|1756 FLLA World Cup squads}}

Each participating squad consisted of 22 players, two of whom were required to be goalkeepers, under the squad allocation in force since [[1740 FLLA World Cup|1740]]. Each participating national association was required to confirm its final 22-player squad with the FLLA no later than seven days before the opening match; late replacements were permitted in the event of serious injury at any time up to 24 hours before a team's first fixture. A total of 704 players were registered for the tournament, of whom 64 were goalkeepers.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.flla.org/world-cup/1756/squad-registration|title=1756 FLLA World Cup: final squad registration list|publisher=[[FLLA]]|date=2 June 1756}}</ref> The 22-player squad rule was used for the last time at the 1756 edition, being replaced from the [[1760 FLLA World Cup|1760 edition]] onwards by a 23-player allocation.

The oldest player at the tournament was [[Verusa|Verusan]] central defender Reinhold Kasspar, who was 37 years and 168 days old at the start of the competition; the youngest was [[Quidic|Quidican]] forward Talin Kestor (20 years and 24 days), who would go on to win the [[#Awards|Best Young Player]] award. The mean age of registered players across the tournament was 26.4 years.

==Venues==
{{Main|1756 FLLA World Cup venues}}

Twelve stadiums in twelve host cities were used in the final tournament, with three venues located in each of the four host countries. Five of the twelve venues had been built specifically for the tournament or substantially redeveloped during the bidding period; the remaining seven were existing top-flight venues that received targeted upgrades to seating and broadcasting facilities under FLLA Council resolution 1751/12. The four-nation venue programme was the largest distributed-host stadium plan in the competition's history at the time.

The opening match was held at the 90,000-seat Nakos National Stadium in [[Nakos]], the largest city in the four host nations, which also staged the second of the two semi-finals on 5 July. The final was held at the Estadio Talvani in [[Talvani]], a purpose-built venue of 84,000 seats inaugurated in March 1756. The two semi-finals were divided between the Nakos National Stadium and the Eserni Arena in [[Eserni]]. The third-place playoff was held at the Takhna Federal Stadium in [[Takhna]].<ref name="flla-venues">{{cite web|url=https://www.flla.org/world-cup/1756/venues|title=1756 FLLA World Cup host venues and capacities|publisher=[[FLLA]]|date=21 March 1756}}</ref>

===Team base camps===

Each of the 32 participating squads selected a base camp from a shortlist of 96 candidate sites circulated by the four host associations in November 1755. Most teams opted for camps in or around the larger host cities, with nine squads basing themselves within a one-hour radius of [[Nakos]], seven near [[Talvani]] and six in or around [[Eserni]]. The remaining ten were divided between the smaller host cities and the inter-host border corridor between [[Quidic]] and [[Erkizil]], which became known during the tournament as the "Ankuano belt".

==Innovations==

The 1756 FLLA World Cup introduced a number of regulatory and presentational changes. The four-nation co-hosting model itself was the most significant of these and had no precedent in FLLA World Cup history; the FLLA Council formalised the model retrospectively in resolution 1757/4, providing a procedural template for any future multi-host bid. The competition was also the first at which referees were required to wear standardised electronic communication earpieces during matches, a procedural change adopted by the FLLA Council on 18 February 1755 to facilitate offside and foul reviews between referee and assistants. A third change, the introduction of a written record of substitutions, was incorporated at the request of the [[QUFVL]] in February 1756 and would later be refined into the substitution-slip rule at the [[1760 FLLA World Cup|1760 edition]].

==Format==

The 32 qualified teams were divided into eight groups of four for the group stage, drawn at the [[#Final draw|final draw]] on 9 December 1755. Each group operated on a single round-robin basis, with each team playing three matches; teams were awarded three points for a win, one for a draw and none for a defeat. The top two teams from each group advanced to the [[#Knockout stage|knockout stage]] while the bottom two were eliminated. Tiebreakers between teams level on points were applied in the following order: overall goal difference, overall goals scored, head-to-head record, fair-play points, and, if necessary, a drawing of lots by the FLLA Organising Committee.

In the knockout stage, fixtures were single-elimination ties played over 90 minutes; ties level at the end of normal time were extended by a single 30-minute period of [[wikipedia:Extra time|extra time]] of two 15-minute halves, with a [[wikipedia:Penalty shoot-out (association football)|penalty shoot-out]] used to decide ties that remained level after extra time. Both semi-final losers contested a [[#Third place playoff|third-place playoff]] on 8 July 1756.

==Opening ceremony==

The opening ceremony of the 1756 FLLA World Cup was held at the Nakos National Stadium on 9 June 1756, sixty minutes before the kick-off of the opening match between [[Ztesh]] and [[New Misos]]. Directed by Ztesh stage producer Hekho Wapiski and choreographed by Sarmis Nakamik, the ceremony lasted 31 minutes and featured 1,160 dancers, 240 musicians and a massed entrance representing each of the four host nations. The performance opened with a sequence depicting the four nations of [[Ankuano]] as a single continuous river system, before transitioning to a portrayal of the seven continental confederations of the [[FLLA]] arrayed in a circular formation around the centre circle. The Quidican vocalist Inveth Karro, joined by the Nakos Choral Society, performed the tournament's official theme song "Four Lands, One Field" as the closing item of the ceremony.

Attending dignitaries included the heads of state and government of all four host nations, the President of the FLLA Council, the heads of state of [[Verusa]], [[New Misos]] and [[Raledria]], and 89 ambassadors and senior diplomatic representatives. The ceremony was watched by an estimated worldwide television audience of 2.6 billion people.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.flla.org/world-cup/1756/opening-ceremony|title=Four host nations stage opening ceremony of the 1756 FLLA World Cup|publisher=[[FLLA]]|date=9 June 1756}}</ref>

==Group stage==

The 32 qualified teams were drawn into eight groups of four. Each group operated on a single round-robin basis, with each team playing three matches; the top two finishers in each group advanced to the [[#Knockout stage|knockout stage]] while the bottom two were eliminated. Group rankings were settled first on points (three for a win, one for a draw), then on goal difference and goals scored.

The group stage was the highest-scoring in the competition's history to that point, with 150 goals in 48 matches. Four sides took maximum points from their three matches: [[Emara]] in Group A, [[Quidic]] in Group B, [[Raledria]] in Group G and [[Sanagara]] in Group H. The highest-scoring contest of the round was [[Quidic]]'s 5–4 win over [[Ohtina]] in Group B. The round also produced the tournament's biggest result against the pre-tournament rankings, [[Iquir]]'s 3–2 win over [[Etirha]] in Group G, and the elimination of a host nation: [[Wundry]] finished third in Group H and became the only one of the four host associations not to reach the knockout stage.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.flla.org/world-cup/1756/group-stage-review|title=Group stage review: hosts Wundry eliminated at the 1756 FLLA World Cup|publisher=[[FLLA]]|date=24 June 1756}}</ref>

==Knockout stage==

The knockout stage involved the sixteen teams that advanced from the group stage. Matches still level after 90 minutes were extended by a 30-minute period of [[wikipedia:Extra time|extra time]]; if scores remained tied after extra time, the tie was decided by [[wikipedia:Penalty shoot-out (association football)|penalty shoot-out]]. Three of the eight round-of-sixteen ties and one quarter-final required additional time, and one tie in total was decided on penalties.

===Round of 16===

The eight group winners were drawn against the eight group runners-up, with each match-up pairing teams from different groups. Three of the eight ties required additional time, and one was decided on penalties. The highest-scoring fixture of the round was [[Emara]] 3–2 [[Ohtina]] at the Oshkari Memorial Stadium. The host [[Erkizil]] were eliminated at the Tiraqsi Olympic Stadium, losing 5–4 on penalties to [[Vesozata]] after a 2–2 draw, while [[Quidic]] came from behind to beat [[Terressin]] 3–2 at the Estadio Talvani.

===Quarter-finals===

The four quarter-finals produced one of the highest-scoring knockout fixtures in the competition's history when [[New Misos]] beat [[Emara]] 6–5 at the Mihkose Sports Complex, a result featuring a hat-trick by New Misos forward Sebrek Galenas. [[Raledria]] overcame [[Verusa]] 4–3 at the Tiraqsi Olympic Stadium, [[Quidic]] beat fellow hosts [[Ztesh]] 3–2 at the Estadio Talvani in the first all-host knockout fixture in FLLA World Cup history, and [[Dual Cenryia]] beat [[Vesozata]] 2–1 at the Mikori Coliseum to reach the first semi-final in their history.

===Semi-finals===

The first semi-final at the Nakos National Stadium was settled inside 90 minutes by [[New Misos]], who beat [[Raledria]] 2–1 through goals from Sebrek Galenas and Marin Sorvel to reach their first final since [[1748 FLLA World Cup|1748]]. The second semi-final at the Eserni Arena required extra time; [[Quidic]] and [[Dual Cenryia]] were level at 2–2 after 90 minutes before a 106th-minute strike from Quidican forward Talin Kestor put the hosts into the final, setting up the first FLLA World Cup final contested by [[Quidic]].

===Third place playoff===

The third-place playoff was contested between the two losing semi-finalists at the Takhna Federal Stadium on 8 July. [[Dual Cenryia]] beat [[Raledria]] 3–2 to claim the first FLLA World Cup medal in their history, with goals from Aldo Vossen, Kel Renstrom and Joran Halvik; [[Raledria]], the top-ranked side in the tournament, finished fourth after replies from Niall Brask and Corwen. The result was recorded by the FLLA as the tournament's second-biggest upset against the pre-tournament rankings.

===Final===
{{Main|1756 FLLA World Cup final}}

The final was contested between [[Quidic]] and [[New Misos]], the Group B winners and Group D runners-up respectively. [[Quidic]] entered the match having scored 21 goals in their five previous fixtures, while [[New Misos]] had reached the final having won three of their four knockout ties by a single goal. Quidic won the match 1–0 to claim their first FLLA World Cup, completing the tournament without a single defeat in normal time across seven matches. The goal, scored in the 64th minute, was the work of Quidican forward Daron Veshani, who turned a Marlen Tavri cross past New Misos goalkeeper Sevren Olbrak from inside the six-yard box.<ref name="flla-final">{{cite web|url=https://www.flla.org/world-cup/1756/final-report|title=Quidic 1–0 New Misos: 1756 FLLA World Cup final match report|publisher=[[FLLA]]|date=9 July 1756}}</ref> The match was also notable for the dismissal of New Misos midfielder Ander Marvik in the 95th minute of normal time, after an off-the-ball incident with Quidican defender Suvan Mihar that drew a straight red card from referee Lassan Vetren; the incident became the subject of [[#Controversies|sustained debate]] in the days following the tournament. The attendance was 83,800.

===Discipline===

The FLLA Disciplinary Committee issued a total of 218 yellow cards and 12 red cards across the 64 matches of the tournament, an average of 3.41 yellows and 0.19 reds per match.<ref name="flla-stats" /> The most-cautioned team was [[New Misos]], with 16 yellow cards and 2 reds across their seven matches; [[Easuhura]] received the fewest among the teams reaching the round of sixteen, with five yellows and no reds across their four matches, helping the team win the [[#Awards|FLLA Fair Play Trophy]]. Five players received red cards in the knockout stage: two in the round of sixteen, one in the quarter-finals, one in the semi-finals and one (Ander Marvik of [[New Misos]]) in the [[#Final|final]] itself.

==Awards==

The Best Player award, formally titled the FLLA Vairan Ball, was awarded by a panel of seven sports journalists drawn from each of the seven confederations to [[Quidic|Quidican]] central midfielder Marlen Tavri, who captained the champions throughout the tournament and contributed five goals and six assists across their seven matches. Tavri was the first Quidican player to win the award. Daron Veshani took the Marskval as the tournament's leading individual scorer with eight goals, two clear of his nearest challengers.<ref name="flla-awards" />

The Bastion, awarded to the tournament's best goalkeeper, went to [[New Misos|New Misosan]] goalkeeper Sevren Olbrak, who kept four clean sheets across New Misos's seven matches, including in the round of sixteen against [[Genaire]] and in the final against [[Quidic]]. Quidican forward Talin Kestor, 20 years old at the start of the tournament, was named Best Young Player after scoring five goals, including the extra-time winner in the [[#Semi-finals|semi-final]] against [[Dual Cenryia]]. [[Easuhura]] received the Fair Play award after finishing the tournament with the fewest disciplinary points of any of the sixteen knockout-stage participants.

==Preparations and costs==

The total budget allocated to the 1756 FLLA World Cup by the four host associations and the governments of [[Erkizil]], [[Quidic]], [[Wundry]] and [[Ztesh]] was {{lahn}}1.68&nbsp;billion. Of this, {{lahn}}1.01&nbsp;billion was directed towards stadium construction and renovation across the twelve venues, {{lahn}}410&nbsp;million towards transport and border-crossing upgrades, and {{lahn}}260&nbsp;million towards operational expenditure including security, broadcasting infrastructure and the volunteer programme. The transport allocation funded the [[Talvani]]–[[Nakos]] high-speed link (opened in stages between November 1755 and March 1756) and an inter-host visa-free travel programme in force for the duration of the tournament. Per-venue capital costs averaged {{lahn}}84&nbsp;million across the twelve stadiums, a figure later cited by FLLA reviewers as comparatively low by the standards of single-host editions, reflecting the wider use of existing top-flight venues.<ref name="flla-costs">{{cite web|url=https://www.flla.org/world-cup/1756/financial-review|title=1756 FLLA World Cup: organising committee financial review|publisher=[[FLLA]]|date=18 August 1756}}</ref>

Five of the twelve venues, comprising the Estadio Talvani, the Eserni Arena, the Vellikar City Stadium, the Reeveta Sports Park and the Oshkari Memorial Stadium, were either newly built or extensively redeveloped for the tournament. The newest, Estadio Talvani, was inaugurated on 12 March 1756, three months before the opening match. Total stadium construction overran the original budget by 8&nbsp;per&nbsp;cent, primarily because of cost escalation at the Estadio Talvani and the Eserni Arena; the smaller per-venue capacities adopted in the four-nation bidding plan limited the absolute scale of the overrun.

The combined security operation involved 36,000 police and military personnel deployed across the twelve host cities of the four host nations, the largest such deployment in the competition's history at the time. A specific cross-border policing protocol, negotiated by the four host associations and ratified at QUFVL level in October 1755, set the operational framework for inter-host movement and information sharing for the duration of the tournament. No serious incidents were reported during the competition.

Total tournament revenue, audited by the FLLA in August 1756, was {{lahn}}2.43&nbsp;billion, against costs of {{lahn}}1.68&nbsp;billion, yielding a net surplus of {{lahn}}750&nbsp;million.<ref name="flla-costs" /> The FLLA's standard 18&nbsp;per&nbsp;cent host-association allocation returned {{lahn}}437&nbsp;million to the four host associations, distributed in shares of {{lahn}}131&nbsp;million each to the Quidican and Ztesh associations and {{lahn}}88&nbsp;million each to the Erkizil and Wundry associations under a formula reflecting the number of matches staged in each nation.

==Marketing==
{{Main|1756 FLLA World Cup marketing}}

The marketing programme for the 1756 FLLA World Cup was overseen by the [[QUFVL]] in partnership with the FLLA's commercial division, with creative direction by the Talvani-based studio Karina Quidan. The programme included the official emblem, mascot, match ball and theme song (see [[#Symbols|Symbols]] below), a four-nation travelling-trophy tour that visited 38 cities across the four host countries in the year preceding the tournament, and a tiered sponsorship structure of five worldwide partners, twelve host-nation partners and six regional supporters. Total sponsorship revenue across all three tiers was {{lahn}}890&nbsp;million, the second-highest gross sponsorship figure recorded by any FLLA World Cup to date at the time of the tournament.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.flla.org/world-cup/1756/commercial-programme|title=1756 FLLA World Cup commercial and sponsorship programme summary|publisher=[[FLLA]]|date=30 May 1756}}</ref>

==Symbols==
{{Main|1756 FLLA World Cup symbols}}

===Emblem===

The official emblem of the tournament, designed by the Talvani-based studio Karina Quidan, was unveiled on 9 December 1753 in a public ceremony at the [[QUFVL]] headquarters in [[Talvani]]. The design depicts a stylised river dividing into four watercourses, each running through one of the host nations, with the four channels rejoining at the base of a single golden trophy. The four-river motif was drawn from the cartography of the Ankuano river basin shared between the four host nations and was intended to symbolise the unity of the four-nation hosting model. The emblem received the FLLA Council's formal endorsement in March 1754 after a six-week consultation period with the seven confederations.

===Mascot===

The official mascot of the 1756 FLLA World Cup, named '''Lirran''', is an anthropomorphic Ankuano river otter dressed in a four-colour panel jersey representing each of the host nations' national colours. The mascot was selected by a four-nation public vote organised by the [[QUFVL]] in the spring of 1754, with four candidate designs presented to voters across the four host countries and in print; Lirran prevailed over a stylised lahn-tree design ("Talen"), a feathered crane ("Eevra") and a steppe fox ("Marisi") with 38&nbsp;per&nbsp;cent of the 4.1 million votes cast across the four host nations.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.flla.org/1754/mascot-vote|title=Lirran named official mascot of 1756 FLLA World Cup|publisher=[[QUFVL]]|date=18 May 1754}}</ref>

===Match ball===

The official match ball, manufactured by the Talvani-based sports equipment maker Mihasi Group, was branded the '''Inaresa'''. The Inaresa featured a 26-panel hand-stitched construction in a blue-and-cream livery, a presentation chosen to evoke the river-and-water motif of the tournament emblem. The ball was the first FLLA World Cup match ball to use a reduced-panel hand-stitched construction (down from 32 panels), a design that was later cited by FLLA technical reviewers as a precursor to the thermally-bonded constructions adopted from the [[1764 FLLA World Cup|1764 edition]]. A distinct gold-coloured version of the ball, the Inaresa Final, was used in the final, the third-place playoff and the two semi-finals.

===Permanent trophy===

The permanent trophy of the 1756 FLLA World Cup, presented to the winners alongside the rotating [[FLLA World Cup#The Andah Cup|Andah Cup]] at the closing ceremony of the [[#Final|final]], was the '''Eserni''', a 50-centimetre four-cornered cast-bronze sculpture jointly commissioned by the four host associations through the [[QUFVL]] secretariat from the Talvani-based studio Karina Quidan, the same studio responsible for the [[#Emblem|tournament emblem]]. The work takes its name from the [[Eserni]] river of the central [[QUFVL]] basin shared by all four host nations, and depicts four waterways converging on a single golden orb representing the unified hosting model. Cast in four sections, one in each host nation, and assembled at the QUFVL workshop in [[Talvani]] in March 1756, the Eserni was unveiled on 9 May 1756, four weeks before the opening match. Following [[Quidic]]'s [[#Final|1–0 win]] over [[New Misos]], the trophy was transferred to permanent retention by the [[Quidic|Quidican]] federation and is displayed at the Talvani Museum of Sport.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.flla.org/1756/permanent-trophy|title=The Eserni unveiled as 1756 FLLA World Cup permanent trophy|publisher=[[FLLA]]|date=9 May 1756}}</ref>

===Theme song===

The official theme song of the tournament, "Four Lands, One Field", was composed by Quidican musician Sevra Mihasi with lyrics jointly written by Mihasi and the vocalist Inveth Karro, who also performed the track. The studio recording was released on 9 March 1756 and topped the charts of all four host nations across the months of April and May 1756, the first song to lead the official charts of all four QUFVL host nations simultaneously.

==Media==
{{Main|1756 FLLA World Cup broadcasting rights}}

The 1756 FLLA World Cup was broadcast in 148 countries by 47 official television partners and a further 19 official radio partners.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.flla.org/world-cup/1756/broadcast-partners|title=1756 FLLA World Cup: official broadcast partner list|publisher=[[FLLA]]|date=20 May 1756}}</ref> Domestic broadcasting rights in the four host nations were held by a joint consortium of the Quidican National Network (QNN), Ztesh Federal Broadcasting (ZFB), Wundry Public Broadcasting (WPB) and the Erkizil National Broadcaster (ENB), which produced the host feed jointly and screened all 64 matches across their terrestrial networks. The international rights for the [[AYFVL]] region were held by [[Emara|Emaran]] public-service broadcaster ECN; the [[ATFVL]] rights by the [[New Misos|New Misosan]] National Network (NMNN); and the [[ACFVL]] rights by a four-broadcaster consortium led by Estijan's national broadcaster ETP.

The final between [[Quidic]] and [[New Misos]] was the most-watched television broadcast in [[Quidic|Quidican]] history at the time, drawing a peak audience of 31.4 million viewers (representing approximately 78&nbsp;per&nbsp;cent of the active television audience in the country). Worldwide, the FLLA reported a cumulative live broadcast audience for the tournament of 2.6 billion individual viewers across all matches, with 1.2 billion individuals tuning in to at least part of the final.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.flla.org/1756/audience-summary|title=1756 FLLA World Cup viewership summary|publisher=[[FLLA]]|date=14 August 1756}}</ref>

===Attendance===

Cumulative attendance across the 64 matches of the tournament was 3,367,000 spectators, an average of 52,609 per match. The highest single-match attendance was the 88,300 recorded at the [[#Semi-finals|first semi-final]] between [[New Misos]] and [[Raledria]] in [[Nakos]], just below the Nakos National Stadium's listed all-seater capacity of 90,000; the lowest was the 38,900 attending the Group F fixture between [[Verusa]] and [[Ucrua]] at the Reeveta Sports Park on 22 June.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.flla.org/world-cup/1756/attendance|title=1756 FLLA World Cup: match-by-match attendance record|publisher=[[FLLA]]|date=12 August 1756}}</ref>

Across the tournament, attendance averaged 58,200 in the knockout stage and 50,170 in the group stage. The three highest single-match attendances of the tournament were all recorded at the Nakos National Stadium, with the first semi-final, the [[Ztesh]] v [[Taval]] round-of-sixteen tie and the opening match all drawing crowds in excess of 84,000.

==Controversies==

The most prominent dispute of the tournament arose from the [[#Round of 16|round-of-sixteen]] tie between [[Vesozata]] and [[Erkizil]] at the Tiraqsi Olympic Stadium on 28 June, the so-called "Tiraqsi affair". After a 2–2 draw across 120 minutes, [[Vesozata]] won the resulting penalty shoot-out 5–4 to eliminate the host [[Erkizil]]; in the immediate aftermath, the Erkizil Arraby Association lodged a formal protest with the FLLA citing video evidence that referee Aakash Sharma had ordered two of Vesozata's shoot-out kicks retaken after movement by the Erkizil goalkeeper that was not, in the association's view, addressed by the laws of the game then in force. On 29 June, the FLLA Disciplinary Committee, convening in special session in Talvani, declined to void the shoot-out, ruling that the retaken kicks fell within the referee's discretion, and the result stood.<ref name="flla-tiraqsi">{{cite web|url=https://www.flla.org/world-cup/1756/disciplinary-tiraqsi|title=FLLA Disciplinary Committee upholds Vesozata–Erkizil shoot-out result|publisher=[[FLLA]]|date=29 June 1756}}</ref>

The Erkizil Arraby Association sought arbitration before the Court of Arraby in Faramozan, which on 1 July upheld the Disciplinary Committee's decision and declined to order a replay. The FLLA published a full review of the procedural conduct of the shoot-out in October 1756, concluding that referee Sharma's actions had been "within the laws but inconsistently applied" and recommending standardisation of shoot-out procedures across all FLLA competitions; the recommendation was adopted by the FLLA Council in resolution 1756/19 on 14 November 1756.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.flla.org/news/1756/shoot-out-procedure-review|title=FLLA review of the Tiraqsi affair recommends standardised shoot-out procedures|publisher=[[FLLA]]|date=14 November 1756}}</ref>

A second incident, the dismissal of New Misos midfielder Ander Marvik in the 95th minute of the [[#Final|final]] for an off-the-ball collision with Quidican defender Suvan Mihar, became a sustained subject of public debate in the days following the tournament. Broadcast footage subsequently confirmed contact between the two players away from play; the New Misos Arraby Association formally complained that the referee Lassan Vetren and his assistants had been unable to view the incident in real time and had ruled on it after consulting the fourth official, an action not unambiguously permitted under the regulations then in force. The FLLA Disciplinary Committee declined to entertain the complaint on 13 July, citing the finality of on-field decisions under the laws of the game. The Marvik dismissal would later be cited by the FLLA Refereeing Committee as a key motivation for the introduction of standardised electronic communications protocols at the [[1760 FLLA World Cup|1760 edition]].

==Aftermath==

[[Quidic]]'s victory was the first FLLA World Cup ever won by a Quidican side. The result was widely celebrated in Quidic, where the team's homecoming parade through central [[Talvani]] on 11 July 1756 drew an estimated crowd of 4.6 million along an eight-kilometre route from the Quidican federal palace to the Estadio Talvani.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/andah/quidic-world-cup-parade|title=Millions line Talvani streets as Quidic celebrate first World Cup|publisher=BBC News Andah|date=11 July 1756}}</ref> [[Dual Cenryia]]'s run to third place was the best result by a [[MAFVL]] side at a FLLA World Cup since the confederation's [[1740 FLLA World Cup|1740]] participation and was widely regarded as the breakout performance of the tournament. The defending champions [[Praesyu]], who had won the [[1752 FLLA World Cup]] in [[United Delet]], did not take part, having failed to come through [[AYFVL]] qualifying.

As reigning champions, Quidic qualified automatically for the [[1760 FLLA World Cup|subsequent 1760 edition]] under the FLLA's defending-champion exemption then in force; Quidic were drawn into Group D at the 1760 tournament and were eliminated in the group stage, finishing fourth in their group. The 1760 edition, hosted by [[Ukhdari]], was won by [[Verusa]].

Across the four host nations, the tournament was judged an organisational success. An independent post-event report jointly commissioned by the four host associations and published in November 1756 estimated the net economic contribution to the four host economies at {{lahn}}4.2&nbsp;billion, against gross public expenditure of {{lahn}}1.68&nbsp;billion across infrastructure and operations.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.globaltradeunion.org/database/1756/quian-host-economies|title=Economic output of the four 1756 FLLA World Cup host economies|publisher=[[Global Trade Union]]|date=18 November 1756}}</ref> International visitor arrivals across the four host countries over the tournament period totalled 1,060,000, the highest cumulative tournament-period visitor figure recorded in the [[Quian Union]] up to that date. The cross-border travel and policing arrangements introduced for the tournament were retained on an extended basis after the closing ceremony and formed the procedural foundation for the later [[Quian Union]] free-movement protocol of 1763.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.qufvl.org/1756/joint-impact-report|title=1756 FLLA World Cup joint post-event economic impact report|publisher=[[QUFVL]]|date=18 November 1756}}</ref>

The next edition of the FLLA World Cup, the [[1760 FLLA World Cup]], was awarded to [[Ukhdari]] at the FLLA Council meeting of 4 February 1754, before the start of the 1756 tournament. The four-nation hosting model introduced at the 1756 edition was retained as a procedural option for future bids; the substitution-record innovation introduced at the 1756 tournament was retained at the 1760 edition and refined into the written-slip protocol used from that competition onwards.
